newsitem.title: USA: Kansas rains halt wheat harvest, may lower quality.
newsitem.headline: Kansas rains halt wheat harvest, may lower quality.

text.p: Heavy rains halted wheat harvesting Thursday in Kansas and northern Oklahoma, and agronomists said Thursday that the accompanying strong winds and hail may lower quality and quantity of the crop.

"Rains at harvest time are not only a problem... for the farmer trying to get wheat out of his fields, they can affect the end-user, too, in terms of quality" said Jim Shroyer, extension agronomist at Kansas State University.
Shroyer said he expected the winds and hail would cause obvious problems like lodging and shattering, which occurs when the grain is knocked out of the wheat heads.
But Shroyer also said some damage to the crop would not be immediately visible to the naked eye.

"When you get rains at maturity stage and then you get several days of dryness and then you get rain again, the seedcoat swells and shrinks... and then that influences the test weights," Shroyer said. "Farmers then can get penalized for having test weight problems."
Rain amounts of 0.5 to 1.5 inches fell over much of southwest and central Kansas, with greater amounts in localized areas, said Joel Burgio, Weather Services Corp meteorologist.
"This was very unfavorable for the harvest," Burgio said.
The storms also featured 60- to 70-mph winds and one- to 1-3/4-inch hail.

But despite the problems that could evolve from the recent rains, Kansas' wheat crop was turning out better than many in the grain industry had anticipated. Sources said the crop had mostly shrugged off the damaging effects of a late-season freeze thanks to cool, wet weather during late April and May.
"This is the best dead crop I ever saw," said Stewart Duncan, Kansas State University extension crops and soils specialist for south central Kansas.

"Yields have been very very good, and quality is better than good, too," Duncan said. "There have been tremendous test weights -- 63- or 64-lb test weights. Yields are up -- as a general rule we're running above county averages. I've heard... of whole fields that were 60, 70 and even 80 bushels (per acre) in a few cases," Duncan said.
